1. The animation shows how often US consumer prices (CPI-U) have risen at a given yearly rate over history. It compares bars for "raise a year" levels of 2%, 3%, 3.1% and 6.38%. Each bar is the share of historical stretches in which that happened. It is labeled "US only · history, not a forecast."

2. Bars are added one at a time, from the bottom up. First is 2% a year, with 2.4% of stretches. Next is 3%, with 42.4%. Then 3.1%, which is labeled "half," meaning about half of stretches. Last is 6.38%, which is labeled "all · Carl's stretch," meaning every stretch. The last two frames carry an "ILLUSTRATIVE" tag. A dotted line marks "half" and another marks "all stretches."

3. As I read it, the share of historical stretches that cleared a given yearly price rise grows as the rate goes up. Only about 2.4% of stretches had at least 2%. About 42.4% had at least 3%. About half had at least 3.1%. All stretches had at least 6.38%, which is the "Carl's stretch" case. The caption in frame 4 calls 3.1% "a median of the past, not an expectation." The figures are historical, and the "ILLUSTRATIVE" tag means the last bars are an example rather than a prediction. I can't tell exactly what "stretches" or "Carl's stretch" refer to, because the frames don't define them.

4. The frames give no explicit advice. A viewer might infer that prices have often risen faster than 2% to 3% a year. That could matter for a payout that doesn't adjust for inflation, which is the choice you face between your two annuity options. But the frames never mention annuities or payouts, so that is my own reading.

5. The animation did not suggest that advice. It only shows the history and warns it is not a forecast. The annuity link comes from your situation, not from the frames.
